title: Reading stitch tops — both loops, front loop, back loop
subtitle: What you're actually inserting into and why it changes the fabric
excerpt: Every standard crochet stitch has two loops at the top — a front loop and a back loop — forming a V. Standard crochet inserts under both loops. Front-loop-only and back-loop-only insertions each use one loop and leave the other free as a visible ridge. This tutorial explains how to identify and choose the loops.

glossaryTerms.definition: The standard crochet insertion: hook passes under both the front and back loops of the stitch top V simultaneously. Used unless the pattern specifies FLO or BLO.

content.text: is the standard crochet default. The top of every crochet stitch has two yarn strands forming a V — the front loop, which sits nearest to you as you hold the work, and the back loop, which sits away from you. Working under both gives a solid fabric with no free strands. Choosing one or the other changes the texture.
Hold the work with the right side facing you. Look down at the top edge of the last row.
The front loop is the strand of the V that angles toward you — the one closest to the hook when the work faces you.
The back loop is the strand that angles away from you — it sits slightly behind the front loop.
Both loops = insert under both strands of the V at once (standard).
FLO = insert under the front strand only, leaving the back strand visible on the other side.
BLO = insert under the back strand only, leaving the front strand visible as a raised ridge.

items.symptom: After the first few rows it's hard to see which loop is which
items.cause: Using a dark or fuzzy yarn that obscures the stitch definition
items.fix: Use a smooth, light-coloured DK yarn when learning to read stitch tops. The V of each stitch top is much clearer in smooth yarn under good light.

content.text: FLO dc and BLO dc go into the detail of working single-loop stitches — how they affect the fabric texture and where they are used. Waistcoat stitch bypasses both top loops entirely and inserts into the vertical body of the stitch, producing a completely different result.
